question: Mr. Osei has a new intermediate class and wants to teach it well. He gives every student an online questionnaire that sorts them into visual, auditory, and kinesthetic learners, and he plans to prepare three separate versions of each lesson so that each student receives instruction matched to their diagnosed style. A colleague asks whether this is the best use of his planning time. Drawing on what the course teaches about learner differences and about lesson planning, what should Mr. Osei do instead, and why?
answer: Mr. Osei is about to spend a large amount of planning time on the one step the evidence does not support. Sorting students by a diagnosed style and then matching instruction to that style is the meshing hypothesis, and Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork (2008) found no adequate evidence that identifying a learner's preferred style and then matching instruction to that style produces better learning outcomes. The mistake is precise, and it is worth naming precisely: the finding is not that individual differences are imaginary, but that diagnosing a fixed style and then restricting each student's instruction to fit that diagnosis does not produce the predicted benefit. Building three parallel single-channel versions of every lesson would multiply Mr. Osei's workload while narrowing each student's access to the material. What Mr. Osei should do instead is plan one lesson for the whole class that moves through a variety of activity formats, so that every student meets the content through more than one route rather than being routed to a single channel. This is the course's evidence-consistent recommendation for honoring real learner differences, and it is also sound lesson planning: a single well-staged lesson that combines visual, spoken, and hands-on work gives Carlos, Wei, Priya, and everyone else several ways into the same material without any questionnaire. The instinct behind Mr. Osei's plan, paying attention to students as individuals, is a good one; the diagnostic-matching method he has chosen to act on it is the part to drop.
anchor: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork (2008) found no adequate evidence that identifying a learner's preferred style and then matching instruction to that style produces better learning outcomes.
rubric: Rubric (10 points): identifies the sort-and-match (meshing) approach as the unsupported step (2); cites Pashler et al. 2008, no adequate evidence for style-matched instruction (2); preserves the correct point that learner differences are real and it is the diagnose-and-restrict method that fails (2); recommends building format variety into one whole-class lesson instead of three style-matched tracks (3); coherent answer connecting the learner-differences evidence to the planning decision (1).
